extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency counsel, and courts evaluating notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze whether a final administrative rule is a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule under APA §553(b), focusing on fair notice, procedural adequacy, and appropriate judicial remedies. Uses the WOTUS proposed/final rule as a case study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth doctrine (basic requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine states that an agency's final rule should be a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibits agencies from using the comment period as a "carte blanche to establish a rule contrary to its original proposal." The doctrine balances agency flexibility and public fair notice; the objective is fair notice without imposing an unreasonable burden on the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §553(b) informal rulemaking procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 553(b) requires agencies to publish a general notice in the Federal Register and to publish the 'terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: publish NPRM with sufficient terms/description, receive public comments, and publish a final rule that incorporates agency expertise and public comment. Compliance with these steps is a prerequisite for logical outgrowth analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific, case-by-case inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical outgrowth is inherently a fact-specific inquiry; each proposed/final rule pair must be evaluated on its own facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single categorical test; nonetheless, grouping similar procedural cases into categories can assist analysis and prediction of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair notice standard — 'should have anticipated' formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts often validate a final rule if interested parties 'should have anticipated' that a change from the proposed to final rule was possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anticipation standard measures whether reasonable commenters could foresee the change; if so, lack of additional notice may be excused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair notice limitation — public need not 'divine the unspoken thoughts' of the agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is not required to infer unstated agency intentions; agencies must provide sufficient disclosure so commenters are not forced to guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a floor for how explicit an NPRM must be; vague or wholly implicit shifts in policy risk invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency contemplating a specific change (affirmative category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will uphold a final rule when the NPRM expressly asks for comment on a particular issue or otherwise makes clear the agency was contemplating a specific change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: NPRM listing specific options (e.g., 5 hours, 8 hours, or other) and the final rule selecting one (8 hours) fits this category. If the agency offered concrete alternatives and solicited comment, selecting among them is a logical outgrowth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on establishing a rule contrary to original proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not use the notice-and-comment period as a means to promulgate a final rule that is contrary to the original proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit limit on agency flexibility; courts evaluate whether the final rule departs so far that commenters lacked fair notice and opportunity to comment on the introduced change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of minor changes learned from comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor changes made in response to comments do not necessarily require a new round of notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be 'absurd' to require new notice for minor edits; agencies must be able to learn from comments and make reasonable adjustments without restarting the process. Whether a change is 'minor' is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of procedural and substantive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural defects (e.g., failure of notice) are a distinct inquiry from the substantive validity of the agency's statutory interpretation or constitutionality of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may remedy procedural failures without resolving or invalidating the agency's underlying substantive positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial remedies for logical outgrowth/procedural failures
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency fails to follow proper procedure, the court's remedy can be a complete remand, a partial remand, or a remand without vacating the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The default remedy is remand to the agency to comply with APA procedures. Courts may tailor remedies considering social costs and private reliance interests; sometimes they remand only the elements lacking proper process or leave a rule in place while ordering procedural cures.
